title: Christians of the Middle East
hook: the oldest churches, now shrinking; Coptic workers killed in Libya for their faith

segments.voice: Yesterday, Latin America, and a Gospel passed around the benches of a tin-roofed chapel. Your line was the bible read by the poor. Did you read a passage with anyone? Day nine hundred eighty.

"And the disciples were called Christians first in Antioch." That's a line from the book of Acts, and Antioch was a real city in what is now southern Turkey, near the Syrian border. So the name itself was first spoken in the Middle East. This week we've traveled the map, to Africa, to Korea, to China, to Latin America. We end the week where the story began, with churches that were never brought in from somewhere else, because they were there from the start. Today, Christians of the Middle East.

In the early chapters of Acts, followers of Jesus are already in Jerusalem, Damascus and Antioch, long before Paul reaches Rome. Churches in those lands still trace themselves to that beginning, churches with long names and longer memories. The Coptic church in Egypt. The Syriac churches. The Assyrian and Chaldean churches of Iraq. The Maronites of Lebanon. The Armenians. Some of them still pray in Syriac, a form of Aramaic. Aramaic is the language Mark preserves when Jesus takes a dead girl by the hand. In the King James Bible: "Talitha cumi; which is, being interpreted, Damsel, I say unto thee, arise." Mark kept the sound of his words. These churches keep its family of words in their worship. They are not new arrivals, and they are not a foreign import. They are what was there first. And in place after place they are fewer than their grandparents knew. War, pressure and poverty have pushed families to leave, and some villages that once filled a church now have few Christian households left. Some have stayed at great cost. In Libya, a group of Coptic Christian workers, with a man from Ghana among them, were seized by an extremist group and killed for being Christians. The video their killers made was meant to frighten. Others who watched it noticed something else: men on a beach, some praying the name of Jesus as they died. The Coptic Orthodox Church counts them as martyrs, and some of their families said publicly that they forgave. The oldest churches have been carrying this for a long time, and they are still praying in the old words.
screen: `THE MARTYRS ON THE BEACH IN LIBYA.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: travel back to the beginning. Settle, and breathe. Picture three places, one at a time. Egypt: a crowded church in Cairo, incense in the air. Iraq: a village church on the plain near Mosul, families coming home to repair it. Syria: a stone chapel with Aramaic words carved over the door. Stay a few breaths in each. If you pray, you can pray for Christians in Egypt, Iraq and Syria, and for everyone in those countries who longs for peace. If you don't, simply hold each place in mind with good will, and remember that people there are praying this hour too. The bell holds the time.
Antioch. The city in the Middle East where the name Christian was first used, home to churches that still pray in a form of the language Jesus spoke.

Your line: the oldest churches. This week went around the world. Today, look up one of those churches by name, Coptic or Chaldean or Maronite, and learn one thing about how it prays. Day nine hundred eighty.

howItsDone: The ancient churches of the Middle East celebrate long liturgies in Coptic, Syriac, Arabic and Armenian, and some Christians elsewhere pray for them by name in Sunday prayers.

notes: Index hook names the year (2015) and the number (twenty-one); per the claims rule both were cut from the script and from the hook field, since no cited text states them. A Keeper may restore them in the hook field if the outline's numbers are wanted (20 Egyptian Copts and 1 Ghanaian, Matthew Ayariga, killed by ISIS in Libya, February 2015).

'some praying the name of Jesus as they died' and 'some of their families said publicly that they forgave': widely reported; the Coptic Orthodox Church added them to its Synaxarium as martyrs. Confirm phrasing.
The killers are named only as 'an extremist group' to avoid any framing against Muslims; confirm.
'Before there was a church in Rome or in Ireland' is a claim of sequence: Acts places disciples in Jerusalem, Damascus (9:2) and Antioch (11:19–26) before Paul reaches Rome. Confirm.
Shrinking: stated without numbers ('fewer than their grandparents knew', 'villages ... now have only a handful of households, or none', 'bells rang for generations'). Confirm fair.
Syriac as 'a form of Aramaic' and Aramaic as the language Jesus spoke (Mark 5:41 preserves Aramaic words). Confirm.
Antioch located 'in what is now southern Turkey, near the Syrian border' (Antakya). Confirm.
Week-end look back: the hook names the week's places (Africa, Korea, China, Latin America).
